claims.source: The prey's movement mimics a moth (Stevenson et al., 1995; Willis and Arbas, 1991) with no ability to hear the bats.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the prey model, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Prey echoes are detected and localized based on biological-relevant assumptions which consider sound reflection and propagation, and hearing physiology.
claims.source: Prey echoes are detected and localized based on biological-relevant assumptions which consider sound reflection and propagation, and hearing physiology (see Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the detection model.

claims.claim: The simulated bats emit search calls with a source-level of 110 dB-SPL at 0.1 m.
claims.source: For example, the simulated bats emit search calls with a source-level of 110 dB-SPL (at 0.1 m, reference 20 μPa)
claims.evidence: This is a specific parameter of the model.

claims.claim: Simulated bats lower their call intensity and adjust other echolocation parameters when approaching prey.
claims.source: and they lower it (and adjust other echolocation parameters) when approaching prey.
claims.evidence: This is a behavior implemented in the model based on known bat behavior.

claims.claim: A successful hunt occurs only when the simulated bat gets within 5 cm from the prey.
claims.source: A successful hunt (i.e. a capture) occurs only when the simulated bat gets within 5 cm from the prey.
claims.evidence: This is a specific criterion in the model.

claims.claim: The simulated bats managed to detect, pursue and capture prey at high rates both when hunting alone and when hunting in a group.
claims.source: The simulated bats managed to detect, pursue and capture prey at high rates both when hunting alone and when hunting in a group (see Figure 1, Video 1 and Video 2 for examples of hunting by simulated bats).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the simulation, with reference to figures and videos.

claims.claim: The movement parameters of the bats in both single and multiple individual scenarios were similar to those of actual bats flying in a flight room.
claims.source: The movement parameters of the bats in both single and multiple individual scenarios were similar to those of actual bats, flying in a flight room (4.5 × 5.5×2.5 m3), suggesting that our model managed to capture the essence of the foraging movement (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a validation of the model against real bat data.

claims.claim: A simulated bat flying in a density of 10 prey items per 100 m2 attacked 5–7 times per 10 s.
claims.source: A simulated bat flying in a density of 10 prey items per 100 m2 attacked 5–7 times per 10 s, similar to the rates reported for P. abramus (Fujioka et al., 2014), a bat with similar foraging behavior, hunting in a comparable environment.
claims.evidence: This is a result from the simulation compared to real bat data from literature.

claims.claim: The JAR was modeled such that whenever the echoes reflected off the closest prey were jammed, the bat shifted its entire frequency range in steps of 2 kHz.
claims.source: The JAR was modeled as follows: whenever the echoes reflected off the closest prey were jammed, the bat shifted its entire frequency range in steps of 2 kHz, upward or downward, to minimize the frequencies' overlap between the masking signal and its own call.
claims.evidence: This is a description of how JAR was implemented in the model.

claims.claim: In all scenarios and for the two different receiver models, the jamming avoidance response did not decrease spectral masking and did not improve detection performance.
claims.source: In all scenarios, and for the two different receiver models, the jamming avoidance response did not decrease spectral masking, and did not improve detection performance according to any of the three criteria defined above. See Figure 2: One-way ANOVA statistics for correlation and filter-bank, respectively: jamming-probability: F1,237 = 2.96, p=0.09; F1,237=2.26, p=0.13; F1,237 = 0.02 p=0.88, ranging error: F1,237 = 0.1 , p=0.76; F1,241 = 0.01, p=0.96, false-alarm: F1,237=0.19, p=0.66, for filter-bank only.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the simulation with statistical support.

claims.claim: Even without any sensory masking, hunting performance significantly degraded as bat density increased due to competition over prey and due to the need to avoid conspecifics.
claims.source: Even without any sensory masking (i.e., in the 'no-masking' condition), hunting performance significantly degraded as bat density increased due to competition over prey and due to the need to avoid conspecifics (Figure 3A–C; see Green lines).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the simulation showing non-sensory effects of group hunting.

claims.claim: The reduction in performance without masking resulted in a maximum decrease of 36%, 57% and 67% in performance when the bats' density increased from 1 to 20 at three prey densities: 3, 10 and 20 prey items per 100 m2, respectively.
claims.source: The reduction in performance was significant in all prey densities and resulted in a maximum decrease of 36%, 57% and 67% in performance when the bats' density increased (from 1 to 20) at three prey densities: 3, 10 and 20 prey items per 100 m2, respectively. See Figure 3 A1–C1, One-way ANOVA, F1, 188 = 64.3, p<0.0001; F1, 188 = 58.9, p<0.0001; F1, 128 = 36.1, p<0.0001, respectively.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the simulation with statistical support.

claims.claim: Sensory masking further hindered hunting under all conditions, but there was no significant difference in performance whether the bats used a JAR or not.
claims.source: Sensory masking further hindered hunting under all conditions, but there was no significant difference in performance whether the bats used a JAR or not (Figure 3, A1-C1, compare blue, black and magenta lines; ANCOVA, F3, 1218 = 2.53, p=0.08, F1, 1581 = 0.57, p=0.56, and F1, 1085 = 0.24, p=0.78, for 3, 10 and 20 prey items per 100 m2, respectively.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the simulation with statistical support.

claims.claim: Jamming mostly occurred during the search phase while, as the bats shifted from the search to the approach phase, the probability of jamming decreased significantly because the prey's echoes become louder.
claims.source: We found that jamming mostly occurred during the search phase while, as the bats shifted from the search to the approach phase, the probability of jamming decreased significantly because the prey's echoes become louder (Figure 3 A3–B3–C3, ANCOVA, for the comparison between search and approach at any bat and prey density: F1, 8527 = 2784, p<0.0001, panels B3-C3 show that less than 15% of the prey echoes are jammed during the approach phase).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the simulation explaining when jamming occurs.

claims.claim: The low probability of jamming during the approach is probably the main reason for the relatively small effect of sensory masking on performance.
claims.source: The low probability of jamming during the approach is probably the main reason for the relatively small effect of sensory masking on performance.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the simulation results.

claims.claim: In a cluttered environment applying a JAR had no significant effect on the hunting performance.
claims.source: We conclude that also in a cluttered environment applying a JAR had no significant effect on the hunting performance, Figure 3—figure supplement 2.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from additional simulations with background clutter.

claims.claim: With 20 bats and 10 prey items per 100 m2, without masking, 34 ± 2% of the capture attempts were successful.
claims.source: With 20 bats and 10 prey items per 100 m2, without masking, 34 ± 2% of the capture attempts were successful (mean ± SE).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the simulation.

claims.claim: When sensory masking was added, the proportion of successful captures significantly decreased to 26 ± 2%.
claims.source: When sensory masking was added, the proportion of successful captures significantly decreased to 26 ± 2% (One-way ANOVA, F1, 198=4.59, p=0.033)
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the simulation with statistical support.

claims.claim: When sensory masking was added, misses became the most substantial cause for failure, significantly increasing to 38 ± 3.5%.
claims.source: and misses became the most substantial cause for failure, significantly increasing to 38 ± 3.5% (One-way ANOVA: F1, 198=68.8, p<0.0001).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the simulation with statistical support.

claims.claim: Increasing the source level improved hunting performance, but only up to a level of ca. 110–120 dB-SPL.
claims.source: Increasing the source level improved hunting performance, but only up to a level of ca. 110–120 dB-SPL, (at 0.1 m) above which the improvement was negligible and insignificant (Figure 4 A1, shows that performance increased significantly when source level increased from 90 to 110 dB: ANCOVA, slope = 0.06 captures/dB, F4, 3815=386, p<0.001; performance did not change when source level increased from 120 to 150 dB: F4, 4795=0.1, p=0.98).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from parameter testing in the simulation with statistical support.

claims.claim: The source level did not affect the masking effect, suggesting that increasing the emission level assists hunting in general and does not assist overcoming the masking problem specifically.
claims.source: Interestingly, the source level did not affect the masking effect (i.e., the reduction in performance beyond the no-masking condition), suggesting that increasing the emission level assists hunting in general (through increasing the detection range) and does not assist overcoming the masking problem specifically (Figure 4 A2; F = 2.45, p=0.16, Pearson linear regression).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from parameter testing in the simulation with statistical support.

claims.claim: Changing the duration of search-calls had no significant effect on the hunting performance.
claims.source: Changing the duration of search-calls had no significant effect on the hunting performance (Figure 4 B1: ANCOVA, F1, 2314=0.15, p=0.69).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from parameter testing in the simulation with statistical support.

claims.claim: Decreasing the hearing threshold significantly improved hunting.
claims.source: Decreasing the hearing threshold (under a constant ambient noise level) significantly improved hunting (Figure 4 C1, ANCOVA, F4, 2395=915, p<0.0001).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from parameter testing in the simulation with statistical support.

claims.claim: Changing the hearing threshold did not significantly change the masking effect.
claims.source: Like in the case of increasing emission level, changing the hearing threshold did not significantly change the masking effect (Figure 4 C2; ANCOVA, F1, 797=2.19, p=0.14).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from parameter testing in the simulation with statistical support.

claims.claim: Only a few studies used a mathematical model to examine the actual chances of being jammed by another bat and how such jamming would affect hunting performance.
claims.source: The jamming problem is one of the most fundamental challenges raised by researchers of echolocation, but, only a few studies (Beleyur and Goerlitz, 2019; Lin and Abaid, 2015; Jarvis et al., 2013; Cvikel et al., 2015b) used a mathematical model to examine the actual chances of being jammed by another bat, and how such jamming would affect hunting performance.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The simulations suggest how even in very high bat-densities, bats can probably capture insects at high rates.
claims.source: Using this approach, our simulations suggest how even in very high bat-densities, bats can probably capture insects at high rates.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the simulation study.

claims.claim: The model follows a conservative approach underestimating the bats' performance, so the result likely reflects the maximum impact of jamming.
claims.source: Because our model follows a conservative approach underestimating the bats' performance (see Materials and methods), this result likely reflects the maximum impact of jamming.
claims.evidence: This is a claim about the model's design and its implications.

claims.claim: Bats' ability to hunt and avoid obstacles in high conspecific density has been documented.
claims.source: Indeed, bats' ability to hunt and avoid obstacles in high conspecific density has been documented (Cvikel et al., 2015b).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about real bat behavior, supported by citation.

claims.claim: The model did not fit any parameters but used parameters based on measurements on real bats or published results.
claims.source: Notably, we did not fit any of the model's parameters – we used parameters that are based on our measurements on real bats or published results.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the model's methodology.

claims.claim: Real bats probably use memory to overcome temporal miss-detections caused by momentary jamming and are thus probably better than the simulated bats.
claims.source: Real bats probably use memory to overcome temporal miss-detections caused by momentary jamming and are thus probably better than our simulated bats.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about real bat capabilities compared to the model.

claims.claim: Much of the interference that bats suffer from when foraging in a group results from competition over prey and from the need to avoid conspecifics, and not from acoustic masking.
claims.source: The two most important results are: (1) Much of the interference that bats suffer from when foraging in a group results from competition over prey and from the need to avoid conspecifics, and not from acoustic masking.
claims.evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the simulation study.

claims.claim: One of the main reasons for the limited effect of acoustic masking is that jamming mostly occurs when the bat is still searching for prey, while once it has detected prey and is closing in on it, prey echoes become loud, and the chances of jamming substantially decrease.
claims.source: One of the main reasons for this is that jamming mostly occurs when the bat is still searching for prey, while once it has detected prey and is closing in on it, prey echoes become loud, and the chances of jamming substantially decrease.
claims.evidence: This is an explanation for the finding, based on simulation results.

claims.claim: Using a spectral JAR is ineffective for solving the jamming problem or even reducing it.
claims.source: (2) Using a spectral JAR, which has been suggested by many previous researchers, is ineffective for solving the jamming problem or even reducing it.
claims.evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the simulation study.

claims.claim: Bats constantly change their signals according to behavioral phase and distance to nearby objects, so even if two bats have the same call repertoire, at any moment in time, their calls are different.
claims.source: The reason for this is that bats constantly change their signals according to behavioral phase and distance to nearby objects. Even if two bats have the same call repertoire, at any moment in time, their calls are different due to their different behavioral phase and because they are likely to have objects at different distances.
claims.evidence: This is an explanation for why JAR is ineffective, based on known bat behavior.

claims.claim: Simulating the second harmonic would have probably made the jamming avoidance response even more irrelevant, because the differences between the calls of different bats would be naturally larger at any moment.
claims.source: Moreover, we only used the bats' first harmonic. Simulating the second harmonic too, thus using signals with more than twice as much bandwidth, would have probably made the jamming avoidance response even more irrelevant, because the differences between the calls of different bats would be naturally larger at any moment (even without a JAR).
claims.evidence: This is speculation about what would happen with a different model design.

claims.claim: In a previous study, no spectral JAR was observed in a bat that uses shallow FM calls (R. microphyllum).
claims.source: Indeed, in a previous study, we did not observe a spectral JAR in a bat that uses shallow FM calls (R. microphyllum) (Cvikel et al., 2015a).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about previous research findings, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Both receiver models revealed the same results regarding the inefficiency of a JAR.
claims.source: Both of the receiver models that we tested revealed the same results regarding the inefficiency of a JAR.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the simulation results.

claims.claim: The correlation-receiver is considered optimal in terms of its detection abilities and probably over-estimates bats' abilities.
claims.source: One of the models (the correlation-receiver) is considered optimal in terms of its detection abilities and probably over-estimates bats' abilities.
claims.evidence: This is a characterization of one of the receiver models.

claims.claim: The correlation-receiver outperformed the filter-bank in all scenarios: it detects more objects and has a lower probability to be jammed by masking signals.
claims.source: As expected, the correlation-receiver outperformed the filter-bank in all scenarios: it detects more objects (see Figure 2—figure supplement 2) and it has a lower probability to be jammed by masking signals (see Figure 2A,B).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of the two receiver models based on simulation results.

claims.claim: The source level actually used by real bats when hunting in a group (ca. 110–120 dB-SPL) gave the best performance in the simulation.
claims.source: We found that the source level actually used by real bats when hunting in a group (ca. 110–120 dB-SPL [Kalko, 1995; Boonman et al., 2013; Kober and Schnitzler, 1990]) gave the best performance in the simulation.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the simulation that matches real bat behavior, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Increasing the source level mainly helped increasing prey detection range and not overcoming masking.
claims.source: Increasing the source level mainly helped increasing prey detection range and not overcoming masking - the masking effect was the same independently of the source level.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from parameter testing in the simulation.

claims.claim: When hunting in aggregations there is no benefit in detecting prey beyond a certain distance because prey that is farther is very likely to be detected and caught by a closer bat.
claims.source: Moreover, increasing the source level beyond 120 dB-SPL did not further improve hunting, probably because when hunting in aggregations there is no benefit in detecting prey beyond a certain distance. Prey that is farther than this distance is very likely to be detected and caught by a closer bat.
claims.evidence: This is an explanation for the finding, based on inference from the simulation.

claims.claim: When hunting under masking background bats increase call intensity.
claims.source: In a previous study, we found that when hunting under masking background bats increase call intensity (Amichai et al., 2015) and others have described similar results (Takahashi et al., 2014; Luo et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about real bat behavior, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Changing the call's duration did not affect the performance.
claims.source: Changing the call's duration did not affect the performance.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from parameter testing in the simulation.

claims.claim: A possible explanation for why call duration does not affect performance is that all simulated bats increased their call duration, so the benefit of own longer calls is balanced with the greater probability of overlapping with conspecific signals.
claims.source: A possible explanation for this is the fact that all simulated bats increased their call duration. Therefore, the benefit of own longer calls is apparently balanced with the greater probability of overlapping with conspecific signals.
claims.evidence: This is an explanation for the finding, based on inference.

claims.claim: The great majority of previous studies reported an upward frequency shift, that is bats always elevated their frequency.
claims.source: Except for a few exceptions (Bates et al., 2008; Luo and Moss, 2017), the great majority of previous studies reported an upward frequency shift, that is bats always elevated their frequency.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of previous research findings, with citations.

claims.claim: The upward frequency shift could be part of the clutter response that is typical for bats when flying in the vicinity of nearby objects.
claims.source: Such a response could be part of the clutter response that is typical for bats when flying in the vicinity of nearby objects. The function of the clutter response (Hiryu et al., 2010) is to improve localization of nearby objects; in this case other bats.
claims.evidence: This is an alternative hypothesis to explain previous findings, supported by citation.

claims.claim: A clutter response is characterized by emitting calls with higher frequencies and by additional signal adjustments such as a decrease in call duration.
claims.source: A clutter response is characterized by emitting calls with higher frequencies and by additional signal adjustments such as a decrease in call duration, as some of these studies indeed reported (Ulanovsky et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is a description of clutter response behavior, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Bats may have approached the playback speaker in playback experiments, thus clutter actually increased in these experiments.
claims.source: One possibility is that bats approached the playback speaker (as many bats do [Cvikel et al., 2015b; Dechmann et al., 2009; Barclay, 1982]) and thus clutter actually increased in these experiments.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about what may have happened in previous experiments, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The Lombard effect, the effect of raising source level in the presence of noise, is well documented in many mammalian species including bats.
claims.source: Another possible explanation for the bats' apparent response is based on the Lombard effect, that is the effect of raising source level in the presence of noise, which is well documented in many mammalian species (Luo et al., 2015; Brumm and Zollinger, 2011; Zollinger and Brumm, 2011; Brumm, 2004; Scheifele et al., 2005), including bats (Takahashi et al., 2014; Amichai et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is an alternative hypothesis to explain previous findings, supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Increasing the emission frequencies could be a by-product of the increase in amplitude.
claims.source: It is also known that increasing the emission frequencies could be a by-product of the increase in amplitude (Titze, 1989; Genzel et al., 2019; Hotchkin and Parks, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about a known phenomenon, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Simulations show that bats' average frequency in the presence of conspecifics would rise by as much as 400 Hz in comparison to when flying alone, although they are not performing a jamming avoidance response.
claims.source: Indeed, our simulations show that bats' average frequency in the presence of conspecifics would rise by as much as 400 Hz (as reported in previous studies) in comparison to when flying alone, although they are not performing a jamming avoidance response (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the simulation that provides an alternative explanation for previous observations.

claims.claim: During encounters with conspecifics the terminal frequencies of nearly all calls were within the predicted transmission repertoire of the individual bats.
claims.source: This result is well-aligned with the findings of Götze et al., 2016. that during encounters with conspecifics the terminal frequencies of nearly all calls were within the predicted transmission repertoire of the individual bats.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison with previous research findings, supported by citation.

claims.claim: The model shows that jamming is less of a problem than previously suggested by most researchers.
claims.source: Our work demonstrates the power of simulations to reveal new insight into complex biological systems that are difficult to examine and analyze otherwise. Our model shows that jamming is less of a problem than previously suggested by most researchers (but see Beleyur and Goerlitz, 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the simulation study.

claims.claim: The model proves that bats can successfully hunt in the presence of other bats without applying any JAR.
claims.source: It proves that bats can successfully hunt in the presence of other bats without applying any JAR
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the simulation study.

claims.claim: Applying a JAR has no significant impact on hunting performance and on prey detection.
claims.source: and shows that applying a JAR has no significant impact on hunting performance and on prey detection.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the simulation study.

claims.claim: The MATLAB model simulates the flight and echolocation behavior of Pipistrellus kuhlii bats.
claims.source: The MATLAB model simulates the flight and echolocation behavior of Pipistrellus kuhlii bats.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model.

claims.claim: Pipistrellus kuhlii is a small insectivorous bat (approximately 5–9 g) common in the Mediterranean region and is often observed in groups of ~5 individuals foraging around a street-light.
claims.source: This small insectivorous bat (approximately 5–9 g) is common in the Mediterranean region and is often observed in groups of ~5 individuals foraging around a street-light (Amichai et al., 2015; Kalko, 1995; Schnitzler et al., 1987; Barak and Yom‐Tov, 1989).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the bat species, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The hunting-ground is a 10 × 10m2 2D area with no obstacles.
claims.source: Our hunting-ground is a 10 × 10m2 2D area with no obstacles.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the simulation environment.

claims.claim: The model consists of three major modules: the prey module, the bat module, and the acoustics module.
claims.source: Our model consists of three major modules: the prey module, the bat module, and the acoustics module.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model structure.

claims.claim: The movement of the targets was simulated by a 'correlated random walk' model, resembling a flight path of a moth.
claims.source: The movement of the targets was simulated by a 'correlated random walk' model, resembling a flight path of a moth (Stevenson et al., 1995; Willis and Arbas, 1991).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the prey movement model, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The linear velocity of simulated prey has an average of 1m/s and changes every 100ms.
claims.source: The linear velocity has an average of 1m/s and it changes every 100ms according to Equation 2
claims.evidence: This is a specific parameter of the prey model.

claims.claim: The simulated prey does not detect or respond to the pursuing bats.
claims.source: The simulated prey does not detect or respond to the pursuing bats.
claims.evidence: This is a simplification in the model.

claims.claim: Each time a bat captures a moth, a new moth is added to the environment at a random position with a random flight direction to keep a constant prey-density.
claims.source: To keep a constant prey-density during the simulation, each time a bat captures a moth, a new moth is added to the environment at a random position with a random flight direction.
claims.evidence: This is a description of how the model maintains prey density.

claims.claim: At the beginning of a simulation, each bat starts foraging in a random position and transmits echolocation calls with 'search' phase parameters.
claims.source: At the beginning of a simulation, each bat starts foraging in a random position and transmits echolocation calls with 'search' phase parameters (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the initial conditions in the simulation.

claims.claim: The foraging behavior of insectivorous bats is divided into three main phases: 'Search', 'Approach', and 'Buzz'.
claims.source: The foraging behavior of insectivorous bats is divided into three main phases: 'Search', 'Approach', and 'Buzz' (Griffin et al., 1965).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about bat foraging behavior, supported by citation.

claims.claim: The model follows the echolocation and hunting behavior of Pipistrellus kuhlii based on field studies.
claims.source: Our model follows the echolocation and hunting behavior of Pipistrellus kuhlii based on field studies (Kalko, 1995; Schnitzler et al., 1987).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model's basis, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The bats in the simulation emit Frequency Modulated (FM) down-sweep signals mimicking P. kuhliis' first harmonic.
claims.source: The bats in the simulation emit Frequency Modulated (FM) down-sweep signals (mimicking P. kuhliis' first harmonic, see Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the echolocation signals in the model.

claims.claim: Before a prey is detected, simulated bats fly according to a 'correlated random walk' path, with a constant linear velocity 3.5 m/s.
claims.source: Before a prey is detected, simulated bats fly according to a 'correlated random walk' path, with a constant linear velocity 3.5 m/s and a random change of direction, sampled from a normal distribution of angular velocities: 0 ± 1 rad/sec (mean ± SD) (Vanderelst and Peremans, 2018; Erwin et al., 2001; Kuc, 1994).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the flight model, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Once a target is detected the bat turns toward the prey by changing its angular velocity according to its relative direction to the target, using a delayed linear adaptive law.
claims.source: Once a target is detected the bat turns toward the prey by changing its angular velocity according to its relative direction to the target, using a delayed linear adaptive law described in Vanderelst and Peremans, 2018; Ghose, 2006.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the pursuit behavior model, supported by citations.

claims.claim: A successful hunt (capture) is achieved when the bat is less than 5 cm from the prey.
claims.source: A successful hunt (capture) is achieved when the bat is less than 5 cm from the prey (Vanderelst and Peremans, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a criterion in the model, supported by citation.

claims.claim: The flight paths, linear velocities, angular velocities, and accelerations of the model were similar to those of actual bats.
claims.source: The flight paths, linear velocities, angular velocities, and accelerations of the model were similar to those of the actual bats (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) implying that our model represents the foraging movement.
claims.evidence: This is a validation of the model against real bat data.

claims.claim: Echoes will only be processed if they cross the auditory threshold set to 0 dB-SPL based on the literature.
claims.source: Echoes will only be processed if they cross the auditory threshold set to 0 dB-SPL based on the literature (Boonman et al., 2013; Poussin and Simmons, 1982; Coles et al., 1989; Popper and Fay, 1995)
claims.evidence: This is a parameter in the model, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The correlation-receiver is based on a similarity between the bat's own transmitted calls and the received signals.
claims.source: The correlation-receiver is based on a similarity between the bat's own transmitted calls and the received signals (Denny, 2004; Saillant et al., 1993).
claims.evidence: This is a description of one receiver model, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The filter-bank receiver is based on the bat hearing model and consists of an 80-channel gammatone filter-bank with frequency bandwidths simulating the tuning curve of the inner-ear.
claims.source: The filter-bank receiver is based on the bat hearing model described in Weißenbacher and Wiegrebe (2003) (Weissenbacher and Wiegrebe, 2003). The detector consists of an 80-channel gammatone filter-bank with frequency bandwidths simulating the tuning curve of the inner-ear (Boonman and Ostwald, 2007; Wittekindt et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the other receiver model, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The model intentionally underestimates the bats' actual performance.
claims.source: In general, our model intentionally underestimates the bats' actual performance, and thus real bats are likely to cope with acoustic masking even better than our simulated bats:
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the model's design philosophy.

claims.claim: The model simulated monaural bats, while real bats use two ears with spatial selectivity.
claims.source: (1) we simulated monaural bats, while real bats use two ears with spatial selectivity (Griffin et al., 1963).
claims.evidence: This is a simplification in the model that underestimates bat performance, supported by citation.

claims.claim: The model did not model the effect of reducing masking achieved thanks to directional hearing and referred to as spatial unmasking.
claims.source: We also did not model the effect of reducing masking achieved thanks to directional hearing and referred to as spatial unmasking. Spatial unmasking can improve the detection in the presence of off-axis maskers by up to ca. 30 dB in the Big Brown Bat, Eptesicus fuscus (Sümer et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is a simplification in the model that underestimates bat performance, supported by citation.

claims.claim: The model assumed a low detection threshold (0 dB-SPL), thus the bats were more susceptible to masking.
claims.source: (2) We assumed a low detection threshold (0 dB-SPL), thus the bats were more susceptible to masking (see Figure 4 C2).
claims.evidence: This is a parameter choice that underestimates bat performance.

results.result: The authors developed a comprehensive sensorimotor simulation model of Pipistrellus kuhlii bats foraging for prey in a 2D environment. The model includes three modules (prey, bat, and acoustics) and implements biologically-relevant parameters for echolocation, flight control, and sensory processing based on published literature and measurements from real bats.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C21 and C73-C91 collectively describe the model architecture, parameters, and biological basis. The model design is well-documented with specific parameters (e.g., C19: 110 dB-SPL source level, C21: 5 cm capture distance) that are supported by citations to relevant literature. The modular structure and biological grounding provide a solid foundation for the simulation study.

results.result: The simulated bats successfully detected, pursued, and captured prey at rates comparable to real bats, and the movement parameters (velocities, accelerations) matched those of actual P. kuhlii bats in flight rooms.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C24 and C88 demonstrate model validation against real bat behavior. C23 shows movement parameters matched real bats in flight rooms (with Figure 1—figure supplement 1), and C24 shows attack rates (5-7 times per 10s) similar to P. abramus. This validation strengthens confidence that the model captures essential foraging dynamics.

results.result: Implementing a spectral jamming avoidance response (JAR) in the model did not decrease spectral masking or improve detection performance across multiple criteria (jamming probability, ranging error, false-alarm rate) for both correlation-receiver and filter-bank receiver models.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C26 describe JAR implementation and its lack of effect, supported by statistical tests (C26: multiple ANOVA tests with p>0.05 for all comparisons). C53 confirms both receiver models showed the same result. The statistical evidence is robust across different scenarios and receiver types, strongly supporting the conclusion that JAR is ineffective in this model.

results.result: Even without sensory masking, hunting performance significantly degraded as bat density increased (36-67% reduction depending on prey density), primarily due to competition over prey and the need to avoid conspecifics rather than acoustic masking.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C28 present quantitative results from the 'no-masking' condition with strong statistical support (C28: ANOVA tests with p<0.0001). C47 synthesizes this as a major conclusion. The ability to isolate non-sensory effects through the no-masking condition is a key strength of the modeling approach, and the statistical evidence clearly supports the magnitude of these effects.

results.result: Sensory masking further reduced hunting performance, but JAR provided no benefit. Jamming occurred primarily during the search phase and decreased significantly during approach as prey echoes became louder, which explains the relatively small overall effect of sensory masking.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C31 and C48 describe the phase-dependent nature of jamming with statistical support (C30: ANCOVA F=2784, p<0.0001 for search vs. approach comparison; C29: no significant JAR effect across multiple prey densities). The mechanistic explanation (louder echoes during approach reduce jamming) is logical and supported by the simulation data showing <15% jamming during approach.

results.result: With 20 bats and 10 prey items per 100 m², adding sensory masking decreased successful captures from 34±2% to 26±2% and significantly increased misses from 15±2% to 38±3.5% as the primary cause of failure.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C35 provide specific quantitative results with statistical support (C34: F=4.59, p=0.033; C35: F=68.8, p<0.0001). These results clearly demonstrate the effect of sensory masking on hunting outcomes and identify the mechanism (increased misses). The statistical tests are appropriate and the effect sizes are substantial.

results.result: Increasing source level improved hunting performance up to 110-120 dB-SPL (matching real bat behavior), but did not reduce the masking effect specifically. Beyond 120 dB-SPL, further increases provided no benefit, likely because distant prey would be captured by closer bats in group hunting.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C37 and C56-C58 describe parameter testing results with statistical support (C36: significant improvement 90-110 dB with F=386, p<0.001; no improvement 120-150 dB with F=0.1, p=0.98). C56 notes this matches real bat behavior (110-120 dB-SPL) with citations. The explanation in C58 is logical given the group hunting context. The convergence with real bat behavior strengthens the model's validity.

results.result: Changing call duration had no significant effect on hunting performance, possibly because when all bats increase call duration simultaneously, the benefit of longer calls is balanced by increased probability of overlap with conspecific signals.
results.evaluation: Claims C38 and C60 report the finding with statistical support (C38: ANCOVA F=0.15, p=0.69). C61 provides a reasonable mechanistic explanation based on the model structure. While the explanation is speculative (C61 is marked as INFERENCE), the primary finding of no effect is well-supported statistically.

results.result: Decreasing the hearing threshold significantly improved hunting performance but did not significantly change the masking effect, suggesting improved sensitivity helps detection generally but not specifically for overcoming masking.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C40 present parameter testing results with statistical support (C39: ANCOVA F=915, p<0.0001; C40: ANCOVA F=2.19, p=0.14). The pattern mirrors the source level results, strengthening the overall conclusion that general improvements in detection capability do not specifically address the masking problem.

results.result: In a cluttered environment with background echoes, applying a JAR had no significant effect on hunting performance.
results.evaluation: Claim C32 reports results from additional simulations testing whether clutter would change the JAR effectiveness, with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 2. This extends the main finding to more realistic conditions, though the claim would be stronger with explicit statistical values in the main text.

results.result: Bats constantly adjust their echolocation signals according to behavioral phase and distance to objects, so even bats with identical call repertoires emit different calls at any given moment, making additional frequency shifts from JAR ineffective.
results.evaluation: Claims C50 and C13 provide the mechanistic explanation for why JAR is ineffective. C50 is based on established bat behavior (marked as KNOWLEDGE and INFERENCE), and C13 connects this to the simulation results. This explanation is logical and consistent with the quantitative findings, though it relies partly on inference from the model behavior.

results.result: Simulations showed that bats' average frequency increases by up to 400 Hz when flying with conspecifics compared to alone, even without performing JAR, which aligns with previous field observations and provides an alternative explanation for reported frequency shifts.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C69 present simulation results that reinterpret previous findings. C68 shows the frequency shift with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1, and C69 notes alignment with Götze et al. 2016. This provides a parsimonious alternative explanation for observations previously attributed to JAR, strengthening the paper's argument.

results.result: The correlation-receiver model, considered optimal and likely overestimating bat abilities, outperformed the filter-bank model in all scenarios by detecting more objects and having lower jamming probability.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C55 characterize and compare the two receiver models. C55 provides evidence with references to figures showing the correlation-receiver detects more objects and has lower jamming probability. This comparison is important because if even the optimal receiver shows no JAR benefit, real bats are unlikely to benefit either.

results.result: The model intentionally underestimates bat performance through conservative assumptions (monaural hearing, no spatial unmasking, low detection threshold, long masking windows, no memory), suggesting real bats likely cope with masking even better than simulated bats.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C97 and C43, C46 describe the conservative design choices with supporting citations (e.g., C94: spatial unmasking can improve detection by 30 dB). This transparency about model limitations strengthens the conclusions—if even this conservative model shows bats can hunt successfully without JAR, real bats almost certainly can. The systematic listing of conservative assumptions is methodologically sound.

results.result: The authors propose alternative explanations for frequency shifts observed in previous studies: the clutter response (characterized by higher frequencies when near objects) or the Lombard effect (frequency increases as a byproduct of amplitude increases), rather than intentional JAR.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C67 present alternative hypotheses for interpreting previous literature, supported by citations. However, these are speculative explanations (C63, C65 marked as SPECULATION) for others' findings rather than direct tests. While the hypotheses are plausible and well-grounded in known phenomena (C66-C67 cite the Lombard effect), they remain untested alternatives. The paper would need additional experiments to definitively distinguish between these explanations and JAR.

results.result: The simulations demonstrate that bats can hunt successfully in groups at high densities despite competition and potential masking, without requiring a spectral JAR, and that jamming is less problematic than previously suggested by most researchers.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C12, C14, C42, C70-C71 present the paper's main conclusions, synthesizing results from multiple simulation experiments. These conclusions are well-supported by the quantitative findings presented in other claim groups (particularly the lack of JAR benefit and the phase-dependent nature of jamming). However, C71's use of 'proves' is too strong—models demonstrate plausibility but cannot prove biological reality.

results.result: The authors establish the biological context and define key terms: echolocation enables bats to hunt in darkness, but conspecific calls may interfere with echo detection. Masking signals reduce detection ability through temporal-spectral overlap, while jamming signals completely block echo detection.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5 provide background and definitions. C1-C2 describe established echolocation knowledge with appropriate citations. C3 states the potential interference problem. C4-C5 define masking and jamming with citation support (C4) and methodological reference (C5). These definitions are clear and appropriately grounded, providing necessary context for the study.

results.result: Previous research presents conflicting evidence on spectral JAR in bats: many studies report frequency changes in the presence of conspecifics or playback signals, while several recent studies found no evidence for spectral JAR.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C8 summarize the state of the literature with appropriate citations. C6-C7 cite studies reporting JAR-like behavior, while C8 cites contradictory recent findings. This accurately represents the controversy motivating the study. The citations appear appropriate and the characterization is balanced.

results.result: The modeling approach offers advantages over experiments with real bats: it allows assessment of acoustic input at every instance (currently impossible with real bats) and enables parameter manipulation to test hypothetical scenarios. Few previous studies have used mathematical models to examine jamming probability and its effects on hunting.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C10 and C41 justify the modeling approach. C9 correctly notes current technological limitations in measuring acoustic input at the bat's ear. C10 describes the advantage of parameter control. C41 notes the scarcity of previous modeling studies with citations. These claims appropriately motivate the methodological choice, though C9's assertion that measurement is 'currently impossible' may be slightly overstated—difficult and imperfect would be more accurate.

results.result: The authors reference previous empirical findings to support model assumptions and interpretations: bats can hunt in high density (C44), the model uses measured parameters rather than fitted ones (C45), no JAR was observed in R. microphyllum (C52), and bats increase call intensity under masking (C59).
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C45, C52, and C59 cite previous work to support various aspects of the study. Each claim includes appropriate citations. C45 is particularly important for model credibility—using measured rather than fitted parameters reduces the risk of overfitting. These claims appropriately integrate the current work with existing literature.
